claims.text: A nanoscale graphene interphase on tungsten particles will increase the effective thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite by approximately 20–30%.
The graphene interphase will not compromise the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The graphene interphase will not compromise the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
The initial material is a composite of sintered tungsten particles infiltrated with copper and lacking an interfacial coating.
A conformal nanoscale graphene layer is to be deposited on tungsten particles by CVD before copper infiltration.
CVD temperature and deposition time can be adjusted to control graphene thickness.
Graphene deposition is to be performed at approximately 900–1050°C.
Avoiding excessive CVD temperature will prevent or limit tungsten carbide formation.
Copper infiltration is to be performed at approximately 850–900°C in an inert atmosphere.
The proposed performance should hold at operational temperatures of 300–600°C and under neutron irradiation typical of fusion-reactor environments.
The intervention produces a continuous, finely tuned graphene interphase at tungsten–copper interfaces.
The graphene interphase facilitates efficient phonon coupling across tungsten–copper interfaces.
Graphene has intrinsically high thermal conductivity.
Graphene bridges the tungsten and copper phases through strong phonon coupling.
The graphene interphase reduces tungsten–copper interfacial thermal resistance.
An optimized graphene thickness avoids disrupting metal bonding and thereby preserves mechanical integrity.
An optimized graphene interphase resists irradiation-induced degradation.
Excessively thick graphene films or excessively high CVD temperatures may weaken tungsten–copper bonding and compromise mechanical properties.
